title: The Giant That Saw It Coming
subtitle: Nokia sold four phones out of every ten in the world. It had already built the future in its own labs. Then it lost.

vocab.def: A company that makes and sells mobile phones.
vocab.ex: Nokia was the biggest phone company in the world.

vocab.def: All the people who buy a product, or the business of selling it.
vocab.ex: Nokia was the leader of the phone market.

vocab.def: Another company that sells the same kind of thing and wants the same customers.
The programs inside a computer or phone. The machine itself is the hardware.
vocab.ex: The hardware was good, but the software was slow.

vocab.def: A screen you control with your finger, not with buttons.
vocab.ex: The first iPhone had a touchscreen and no keypad.

vocab.def: The first model of a new product, made to test the idea.
vocab.ex: Nokia built touchscreen prototypes years before Apple.

vocab.def: To feel fear. Afraid of + noun; afraid to + verb.
vocab.ex: Managers were afraid to tell the boss the bad news.

vocab.def: After the right time. Too late = the time has passed and now it is impossible.
vocab.ex: The new phones arrived two years late.

vocab.def: To not win, or to no longer have something.
To continue to live or exist after something bad.
vocab.ex: The company survived, but the phone business did not.

vocab_discuss: What phone did you have ten years ago? Was it better or worse than your phone now?
Have you ever been afraid to tell someone bad news at work or at school? What happened?
Think of a company that was big when you were a child. Is it still big today?

story.heading: Part 1 — The biggest company in the world
paras: In 2007, Nokia was the biggest phone company in the world. Four phones out of every ten came from Nokia. The company was from Finland, a small country in northern Europe, and it was Finland's most famous company.
Nokia phones were very good. They were strong. You could drop them and they did not break. The battery worked for a week.
And Nokia knew about the future. In its labs, it had already built touchscreen phones. It had ideas for app stores and mobile internet. These prototypes existed years before other companies.
In January 2007, Apple showed the iPhone. Apple was a computer company. It knew nothing about phones. The first iPhone was expensive, it broke easily, and it was not very good for phone calls.
People inside the phone industry laughed. They were not stupid: as a phone, the iPhone really was worse. But it was not really a phone. It was a small computer that could also make calls.
tf: In 2007, Nokia sold about four phones in every ten.
Nokia had never built a touchscreen phone before 2007.
The first iPhone was cheap and very good for phone calls.
discuss: Nokia already had the ideas. So why is this story a problem for Nokia?
Why did people in the phone industry laugh at the first iPhone? Give two reasons from the text.

story.heading: Part 2 — Nobody wanted to say it
paras: Nokia tried to answer Apple. It started new touchscreen projects. But Nokia's software was old. It was built for a different time, and changing it was slow and difficult.
The engineers who made the machines were still excellent. But they waited and waited for the software. Deadlines moved from months to years.
Later, researchers talked to many people who worked at Nokia. They found the real problem. It was fear.

Middle managers were afraid to tell their bosses how bad the software was. They were afraid for their money, their jobs and their careers. So at every level, the news became a little better than the truth.

The top bosses saw good reports. So they asked the engineers for impossible things. The engineers could not do them, so they also reported good news. Nobody told a big lie. But the whole company was not telling the truth.

In 2011 the new boss, Stephen Elop, wrote a famous letter to his staff. He said Nokia was like a man standing on a burning oil platform in the sea. Stay, and you die. Jump into the cold water, and maybe you live.
Nokia jumped. It stopped using its own software and chose Microsoft's software instead.
tf: Nokia's engineers were bad at making phone hardware.
Managers did not tell their bosses the truth because they were afraid.
Elop said the company was safe and everything was fine.
discuss: Why did the managers not tell the truth? Was this their fault, or the company's fault?
Elop said: stay and die, or jump into cold water. Was this a good way to talk to his staff?

story.heading: Part 3 — Two endings
paras: The jump did not work. Nokia told everybody that its old phones were finished — but the new phones were not ready for another year. So people stopped buying the old ones, and there was nothing new to buy.
When the new phones came, reviewers liked them. Customers did not. There were already two big systems, Apple and Android, and app makers did not want to build for a third.

In 2013 Nokia sold its whole phone business to Microsoft for about five and a half billion euros. Two years later, Microsoft stopped making phones. The most famous name in mobile phones disappeared from phones.

But there is a second ending. The company Nokia did not die. It stopped fighting for phones and sold network equipment instead — the machines that make mobile networks work. It still does this today, and it makes money.
And Finland survived too. Thousands of Nokia engineers lost their jobs, and many of them started new companies. One of them made the game Angry Birds.

So here is the hard question. Nokia had the technology first. It had the money, the brand and the best engineers. And it still lost. Where did it lose? In the labs? In the software? In the Microsoft decision? Or years before, in a hundred meetings where nobody wanted to give the bad number?
tf: Nokia announced the end of its old phones before the new ones were ready.
The company Nokia does not exist today.
Some engineers who lost their jobs started new companies.
discuss: Nokia told customers the old phones were finished, one year too early. Why was this such a bad mistake?
Nokia lost the phone business but the company survived. Is this story a failure or not? Say why.
Tell the story again in six sentences. Use: used to · tried · was afraid · sold · lost · but.

grammar.name: used to
grammar.heading: used to — things that were true before, but are not true now
explain: This whole story is about a company that used to be number one. English has a special structure for exactly this: something was true in the past, and it is not true now.
Positive: Nokia used to be the biggest phone company. (before yes — now no)
Negative: People didn't use to have touchscreens. (NOT didn't used to)
Question: Did you use to have a Nokia? (NOT Did you used to)
Careful: after did, we write use to, with no d. You cannot hear the difference when people speak, but you can see it when you write.

head: Form
Example
Careful!
rows: Nokia used to sell four phones in ten.
Nokia didn't use to have a competitor.

practice.heading: Complete the sentences about the story
practice.intro: Use used to, didn't use to or still. Read the whole sentence first.
items: Nokia ___ be the biggest phone company in the world, but Apple and Android took the market.
In 2005, phones ___ have touchscreens; they had small plastic buttons.
Nokia ___ makes network equipment today, and the business is profitable.
Kodak and Nokia ___ be national champions in their countries.
Managers ___ tell the truth about the software, because they were afraid.

fix.heading: Find the mistake
items: Nokia didn't used to have a serious competitor.
Did you used to have a phone with buttons?
My grandmother use to work in a factory.
Nokia used to sell phones, and it used to sell network equipment today.
I am used to live in a small village when I was a child.
answers: Nokia didn't use to have a serious competitor. (after "didn't", no d)
Did you use to have a phone with buttons? (same rule, after "did")
My grandmother used to work in a factory. (positive form needs the d)
Nokia used to sell phones, and it still sells network equipment today. (true now = still)
I used to live in a small village when I was a child. ("I am used to" means something different — it means it is normal for me)

speak.label: 1 · Tell the story
paras: Tell me the story of Nokia in your own words. Six or seven sentences is enough.

speak.label: 2 · Then and now
paras: Tell me about something in your life that used to be one way and is different now — your city, your job, your free time, your family.
Use used to at least three times.

speak.label: 3 · Bad news
paras: Nokia's managers were afraid to give bad news. Is it easy or difficult to give bad news where you work or study?
What makes it easier?

speak.label: 4 · Your opinion
paras: Nokia had the best ideas first, and still lost. Why do you think this happens to big companies?
Give one example from your own country.

final: Is it better to be first with a new idea, or second and safer? Why?
Nokia was very important for Finland. What happens to a country when its biggest company fails?
If you were the boss of Nokia in 2007, what would you do differently?
